# Descriptive statistics for the NHANES dataset

The NHANES package on CRAN includes a dataset called "NHANES" that
addresses issues of sampling to permit direct statistical analyses.

Example analyses of the weighted survey data assembled by the National
Center for Health Statistics are available. An example is
[here](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/data/Tutorials/Code/DB303_R.r); also of
interest is the nhanesA package, which leverages a containerized
relational database. A publication is
[available](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11020206/).

Here we use the 'resampled' version for simplicity.

## Software setup

Let's get the necessary software. Use `install.packages` for any
packages you are missing.

```{r lknh, message=FALSE}
library(NHANES)
data(NHANES)
library(dplyr)
library(table1)
library(ggplot2)
nh11 = NHANES |> filter(SurveyYr == "2011_12")
```

## "Table 1"

The `table1` package/function provides a powerful approach to producing
summary statistics. We will focus on the measured quantity "diastolic
blood pressure" as obtained by averaging several repeat measures for
each participant visit.

```{r femd, message=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Basic DBP statistics for females"
#| results: asis
table1(~BPDiaAve|Race3, data=nh11 |> filter(Sex=="female"))
```

```{r mald, message=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Basic DBP statistics for males"
#| results: asis
table1(~BPDiaAve|Race3, data=nh11 |> filter(Sex=="male"))
```

### Exercise 1.

Write and run the *dplyr* code to reproduce the means, standard
deviations and number of missing values for BPDiaAve in each table. The
result should have column names "Sex", "Race3", "mean", "sd", "nmiss".
Records for females should come first and rows should be sorted by race
within gender.

```{r femd, message=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Basic DBP statistics for females"
#| results: asis

nh11 |> 
  group_by(Sex,Race3) |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(BPDiaAve,na.rm = TRUE), #to remove/ignore missing values
    sd = sd(BPDiaAve, na.rm = TRUE),
    nmiss = sum(is.na(BPDiaAve)),
    .groups ='drop'
              ) |>
      arrange(Sex, Race3)

```

### Exercise 2.

Something very implausible is present in the data. Describe it and
reproduce the table1 results and dplyr summaries after "fixing" it.

```{r}
summary(nh11$BPDiaAve)
nh11 |>
  arrange(desc(BPDiaAve))|>
  select(Sex, Race3,BPDiaAve)|>
  head(5)
nh11 |>
  summarise(
    zero=sum(BPDiaAve ==0, na.rm = TRUE),
    missed = sum(is.na(BPDiaAve)),
    total_rows = n()
  )
```

I check the diastolic blood pressure and found multiple participants
have 0 mmHg, which is implausible because they may affect the data
measurement. There are 37 0 mmHg diastolic blood pressure and 719
missing values among 5000 records. So I treat them as missing values.

```{r}
nh11_clean <- nh11 |>
  mutate(BPDiaAve = na_if(BPDiaAve,0))
sum(is.na(nh11_clean$BPDiaAve))
```

```{r}
dplyr_means<- nh11_clean |> 
  group_by(Sex,Race3) |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(BPDiaAve,na.rm = TRUE), #to remove/ignore missing values
    sd = sd(BPDiaAve, na.rm = TRUE),
    nmiss = sum(is.na(BPDiaAve)),
    .groups ='drop'
  ) |>
  arrange(Sex, Race3)
dplyr_means
```

Description: The new dataframe has higher mean and more missing values.

Reproducing table 1:

```{r}
table1(~BPDiaAve|Race3, data=nh11_clean |> filter(Sex=="male"))
table1(~BPDiaAve|Race3, data=nh11_clean |> filter(Sex=="female"))
```

### Exercise 3: Compact estimation procedures for averages

R's built-in modeling functions can save a lot of filtering and
summarization activity. To estimate average diastolic blood pressures
for combinations of race and gender, we can use

```{r dolm1}
lm1 = lm(BPDiaAve~Race3*Sex-1, data=nh11, na.action=na.omit)
lm1$coef
```

The syntax `y ~ a * b - 1` for numerical `y` and factor variables `a`
and `b` is described as fitting "first-order interactions". Subgroups of
individuals are formed for every combination of factor levels, and the
mean value of `y` is computed for each subgroup. The `-1` suppresses an
intercept term.

R uses a peculiar naming convention for the estimated parameters.
`Race3Asian` is used to show that the factor level for Race3 is Asian.
`Sexmale` has a coefficient. This indicates to us that the 'reference'
sex is female. Finally colon is used for combinations of factor values.
We can recover the mean value for Black males by adding the coefficients
for Race3Black, Sexmale, and Race3Black:Sexmale.

Create the compact estimates using the version of the data "repaired" in
Exercise 2 and verify that the estimates from lm recover the dplyr
summaries.

```{r}
lm1_clean = lm(BPDiaAve~Race3*Sex-1, data=nh11_clean, na.action=na.omit)
lm1_clean$coef
```

```{r}
cleaned <- expand.grid(
  Race3 =levels(nh11_clean$Race3),
  Sex = levels(nh11_clean$Sex)
)
cleaned$lm_mean <- predict(lm1_clean, newdata =cleaned)

cleaned
```

```{r}
recover <- cleaned |>
  left_join(dplyr_means, by=c('Sex','Race3'))|>
  mutate(
    difference = lm_mean -mean,
    equal = near(lm_mean, mean)
  )
recover
```

The 'equal' column shows that the estimates from lm recover the dplyr
summaries.

### Exercise 4: Visualizing DBP distributions by age and race

Here is classic R list manipulation and plotting code:

```{r lkmmm}
par(mfrow=c(3,2),las=2,mar=c(5,4,2,2))
ss = split(nh11, nh11$Race3)
tt = lapply(names(ss), function(x) {d = ss[[x]]; 
   boxplot(split(d$BPDiaAve, d$AgeDecade), main=x, ylim=c(0,120))})
```

Write and run the ggplot2 code to produce a similar display.

```{r}
ggplot(data = nh11, aes(x=AgeDecade,y=BPDiaAve))+ # for each graph sets x and y
  geom_boxplot(fill ='grey80',color='black',na.rm=TRUE,outlier.shape=1)+ #boxplot
  facet_wrap(~ Race3,ncol=2) +# split into race and have a 3*2 layout

  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,120))+ #mar=c(5,4,2,2))+
  theme_classic()+
  theme(
    axis.text.x =element_text(angle = 90, hjust =1),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA)
    ) #las =2

```

### Exercise 5: Do ethnic groups have comparable age distributions?

do you see as the most prominent indications of heterogeneity in age
distributions across the different group combinations?

table

```{r lktab}
with(nh11, table(AgeDecade, Race3))
```

lm_age <- lm(Age ~ Race3 * Sex - 1, data = nh11)
ageg <- expand.grid(
  Race3 = levels(nh11$Race3),
  Sex = levels(nh11$Sex)
)
ageg$mean_age <- predict(lm_age,newdata=ageg)
ageg

nh11 |>

expected

### Exercise 6: Cards to Dice

Modify all the quarto and R following to replace draws from a deck of
shuffled cards with tosses of a single six-faced die.

As an example, you might start with code like

```         
die = c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
roll = function(die) sample(die,size=1)
set.seed(1234)
table(replicate(100, roll(die)))
```

to model 100 tosses of a fair die.

We have 100 simulated tosses of a fair six-sided die.

```{r}
die <-1:6
set.seed(1234)
rolls <- sample(die, size=100,replace=TRUE)
table(rolls)
```

## Modeling six-sided die

### Die faces as vectors

We followed online code to produce

```{r do1}
die <-1:6
die
# Combine ranks and suits to make 52 unique cards # 4 suits and 13 ranks in one deck(52)
```

A six-sided die is a vector with 6 elements. This vector "models" the
outcomes of a die toss.

## Draws as samples

With R's `sample` function, we can simulate tossing. We use `set.seed`
to make sure reproducibility.

```{r lkshuf}
toss_die= function(x) { 
   stopifnot(length(x)==6, is.atomic(x)) #atomic vector check if satisfy the condition, no then stop
   sample(x, size=1) #toss once from 6 possible results
}
set.seed(1234)
drs = replicate(2000, toss_die(die)) # toss 2000 times
head(table(drs)) #count number of times each number appear
mean(table(drs)) # mean of freq
2000/6 # the mean that should appear generally with equal prob
```

## A model for fairness

### Intuitions

For a fair die with thorough tossing and replacement, we have an
intuition that each die number has the same chance of being drawn as the
top one.

In 2000 independent tosses, the *expected* number of appearances of each
face is 2000/6(333.33).

### Formalism

Formally, we can abstract from the actual names of the die and represent
the tossing procedure in this way:

Let $i = 1, \ldots, 6$ denote 6 sides.

Let $j = 1, \ldots, 2000$ denote tosses.

Define

$$C_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if toss } j \text{ results in face } i, \\
  0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$

Now define $X_i = \sum_j C_{ij}$. Our statement above about the
intuitive expectation on the number of appearances of any given number
will be written $$EX_i = 2000/6 \text{ for all } i = 1,\ldots, 6.$$

This is equivalent to the following formulation. Let
$p_i, i=1, \ldots, 6$ denote the *probability* (not yet defined in any
formal way) that our toss procedure yields number $i$. Then
$EX_i = 2000 p_i$ for all $i$. For the general case of $n$ tosses,
$EX_i = n p_i$.

## Measuring departure from fairness

A well-established metric for assessing departure from fairness is
called "chi-squared". We will use the symbol $D$ to represent this
measure. Large values of $D$ can be indicative of departure of the
observed frequencies from the expected values.

$$D = \sum_{i=1}^{6} \frac{(X_i - EX_i)^2}{EX_i}$$

We'll implement $D$ as `mystat` and show that it is equivalent to a
quantity computed in R with `chisq.test`.

```{r OmE}
mystat = function(dat, expected) {
  sum((table(factor(dat, levels = 1:6)) - expected)^2 / expected)
}
ExpectedCount = 2000/6
sum((table(drs)-ExpectedCount)^2/ExpectedCount)
chisq.test(table(drs))
mystat(drs, ExpectedCount)
```

Note that `chisq.test` reports the same statistic as `mystat`, but
includes values for `df` (degrees of freedom) and `p-value`. "Degrees of
freedom" refers here to the fact that we have a fixed number of count
categories (6 numbers), and if 5 are known, the value for the 6th can be
deduced -- it is "unfree".

For a fair die, the expected frequency of each face is 2000/6. The
chi-squared has 5 degrees of freedom due to six categories and fixed
total number of tosses.

The p-value is a quantity that, when small, can be indicative of a
departure from the expected outcome of an experiment. We will return to
that concept at a later date.

## Replicating our test of fairness many times

Any given collection of toss events will yield a value of $D$. Different
series will yield different values of $D$, but when the die is fair, the
variation in $D$ is prescribed by the mathematics of probability.

We will make a histogram of 100 replicates of 2000 tosses to exhibit
variation in $D$.

```{r domore}
set.seed(1234)
predist = lapply(1:100, function(x) replicate(2000, toss_die(die))) #replicate 100 times exp. each exp rolls the die 2000 times.
dist = sapply(predist, function(x)mystat(x, expected=2000/6)) #calculate each experiment's chi-square
hist(dist, prob=TRUE) # for histogram of 100 replicates.
```

With 1000 replicates, we get a more pleasing display.

```{r domore2, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(1234)
predist = lapply(1:1000, function(x) replicate(2000, toss_die(die)))
dist = sapply(predist, function(x)mystat(x, expected=2000/6))
hist(dist, probability=TRUE)
```

The form of this histogram (drawn in R with the `probability` argument
set to TRUE) can be approximated by the density of the chi-squared
distribution with 5 degrees of freedom.

```{r lkdens}
hist(dist, probability=TRUE) # y axis is density
lines(1:100, dchisq(1:100, 5)) # generate integer from 1 to 100 for x axis.
```

The "5" fixes the degrees of freedom of the model for which the density
will be drawn.

## Interpret

What's the difference between these two runs?

```{r lkbad}
set.seed(1234)
baddie = die
baddie[1] = 6
newdrs = replicate(2000, toss_die(baddie))
mystat(newdrs, ExpectedCount)
```

```{r lkbad2}
set.seed(1234)
baddie[2] = 6
newdrs = replicate(2000, toss_die(baddie))
mystat(newdrs, ExpectedCount)
```

The difference is the first run has a unfair die, where the probability
of 6 is 2/6(1/3), and the second run has a worse unfair die, where the
probability of 6 is 3/6(1/2). We may have a larger chi-squared
statistic, which show how the chi-squared statistic measures
discrepancies between observed and expected frequencies.
